---

The 13-hour flight was beginning to feel like a 24-hour journey.

Fighting a 180 mph headwind, was like treading water 38,000 feet above the Pacific Ocean, somewhere near the International Date Line.

Desperate for a distraction that might speed up the clock, I flipped through the in-flight entertainment system and began browsing the movie section.

I scrolled over to a category labeled *Critically Acclaimed*.

Almost every title felt like a new release to me.

I had stopped paying attention to movies and television series back in the mid-1990s, leaving a gap in my pop culture knowledge.

But as I browsed, a series of titles caught my eye: *The Matrix*.

I had heard people talk about this movie for decades, but I had never actually seen it for myself.

Settled on the first in the series, one released in 1999.

At 2 hours and 16 minutes, the movie was a great candidate as the distraction du jour.

However, the pacing of the movie mirrored the flight, methodical and unassuming.

I have gotten used to a well defined hero and there was no identifiable hero for the first half of the movie.

Out of boredom and frustration I changed the screen to the flight data screen, least it had a sense of progression and quantified scale to the finish.

---

Then, the story and the flight progression converged.

As our plane skirted the Kamchatka Peninsula and crossed the Sea of Okhotsk, the headwinds eased and we began to pick up speed, cruising steadily toward our destination.

Our hero discovered a singular mission: to rescue his mentor, Morpheus. 

Armed with his training and supported by Trinity, Neo overcame his nemesis, Agent Smith, and the system built to hold him back.

Watching the hero awaken to his purpose reminded me of the core message in Viktor Frankl’s Man’s Search for Meaning:

“It did not really matter what we expected from life, but rather what life expected from us.”

Frankl taught that we must stop asking about the meaning of life in the abstract. 

Instead, we must recognize that life questions us—and we answer through our actions, our choices, and how we meet our responsibilities.

Viktor Frankl learned this in the concentration camps; Neo learned it inside the simulated reality of the Matrix.

Likewise, we too discover meaning by accepting our responsibilities, refining our attitudes, and recognizing that each of us has a unique mission—one that continually unfolds and changes over time.

As Ellie so enthusiastically declared from Charles Muntz’s motto in Up!:

"Adventure is out there!"

And answering that call is where life's true meaning resides.
